reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A disorder in which monoclonal light chains (most often kappa) are deposited in a granular, non-fibrillar, non-organised form throughout the kidney and other organs
It is part of the monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease spectrum and reflects an underlying plasma cell or B-cell clone, sometimes with overt multiple myeloma
Unlike amyloidosis, the deposits are Congo red negative and do not form fibrils on electron microscopy
Renal involvement typically causes proteinuria, often nephrotic range, with hypertension and progressive kidney impairment
The classic glomerular lesion is nodular glomerulosclerosis, which can resemble diabetic nodular disease, so light chain deposition should be considered in nodular patterns without diabetes
Immunofluorescence shows monotypic light chain staining along tubular and glomerular basement membranes, a key diagnostic feature
Evaluation requires serum and urine studies for a monoclonal protein, free light chain assay, and often bone marrow examination to characterise the clone
Treatment targets the underlying clone with clone-directed therapy, since reducing light chain production is central to preserving organ function
reference.pathophysiology: Light chain deposition disease occurs when a clonal population of plasma cells or B cells overproduces a monoclonal light chain that, because of its physicochemical properties, precipitates in a granular non-fibrillar form. These deposits accumulate along the glomerular and tubular basement membranes and within the mesangium, driving mesangial matrix expansion and nodular glomerulosclerosis as well as tubular injury. The deposited light chains are Congo red negative and lack the beta-pleated sheet organisation of amyloid. Continued deposition disrupts the filtration barrier and tubular structures, producing proteinuria and progressive kidney failure, and similar deposits can affect the heart, liver, and other organs.
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation
Serum free light chain assay and ratio
Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence for monotypic light chains and electron microscopy
Congo red staining to exclude amyloidosis
Bone marrow examination to identify and quantify the underlying clone
redFlags: Rapidly declining kidney function or nephrotic-range proteinuria
Features of multiple myeloma (hypercalcaemia, anaemia, bone lesions)
Cardiac or hepatic involvement from extrarenal deposition
New nodular glomerulosclerosis in a patient without diabetes
reference.prognosis: Outcomes depend on the extent of organ deposition and the response of the underlying clone to therapy; effective suppression of light chain production can stabilise kidney function, whereas untreated disease progresses to kidney failure and carries risk from extrarenal deposits.
pitfalls: Mistaking nodular glomerulosclerosis for diabetic nephropathy in a non-diabetic patient
Confusing it with amyloidosis without Congo red and ultrastructural confirmation
Failing to identify and treat the underlying plasma cell or B-cell clone
